name: Data Mapper
intent: Keep domain objects and database tables separate, and let one mapper class translate between them.
scenario: A User has a name and an email. The table stores them in columns called full_name and mail, and one day the column mail is renamed email_address.
problem: The User class reads and writes rows itself. It knows the table and the column names, so every class that touches rows is tied to the schema. Renaming a column breaks code all over the project, and the User cannot be used or tested without a table.
solution: The User is a plain domain object with no idea that a database exists. A UserMapper knows the table, the column names and how to turn a row into a User and back. Callers ask the mapper to find or save users. A schema change is made in the mapper only, and the domain object stays the same.
pain: User reads row columns such as full_name and mail directly
Several classes build or read rows with the same column names
Renaming a column means editing many files
User cannot be created or tested without a table
benefits: Domain objects know nothing about tables
A column rename is a change to one mapper
Domain rules are tested with plain objects, with no database
Objects and tables may have different shapes, such as one object over two tables
whenToUse: Domain objects have real rules and should not depend on storage
The schema and the object model change at different speeds, or have different shapes
You want to test domain logic without a database
whenNotToUse: A simple CRUD tool where each object matches one table and has no rules: Active Record or direct queries are smaller
A small project where one more class per entity costs more than it saves
When your ORM already works as a data mapper: configure it rather than building a second one
pitfalls: Business rules creep into the mapper because it can see every field
Loading an object with many related objects one query at a time (the N+1 problem)
A mapper for every table, even join tables that are not domain objects, adds classes with no meaning
Hand-written mappers fall out of date with the schema unless tests cover them

roles.label: Domain object
roles.description: A plain object with the business data and rules. It knows nothing about tables.

roles.label: Mapper
roles.description: Knows the table and column names, and converts rows to domain objects and back.

roles.label: Table or row
roles.description: The storage shape: column names, types and rows.

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Code that asks the mapper to find or save, and works with domain objects only.

quiz.question: A column is renamed from mail to email_address, and the change touches 12 files that read row.mail directly. What is the best structure to avoid this next time?
options: Name columns more carefully in the beginning, so that renames never happen later on
Keep a document that lists every file that reads each column, and update it with every change
Read columns only in a mapper that returns domain objects, so a rename changes one class
Keep both column names in the table for a year, and let each file move when it is ready
quiz.explanation: The cost came from many files knowing the schema. A mapper is the single place that does, so the rename becomes one edit. Better first names cannot prevent every change, a document does not prevent the edits, and keeping both columns only delays them.

quiz.question: A team builds a mapper class, an interface and tests for each of the 3 tables in an internal admin tool. The tool only lists and edits rows, and has no business rules. What is the likely result?
options: A safer tool, because every table now has a mapper that can be tested separately
More code than the tool needs, since a simple Active Record or direct query would be enough
A faster tool, because mappers cache rows in a way that avoids repeat queries
A tool that is much easier to change, because it can now use any kind of database
quiz.explanation: A mapper pays off when domain objects have rules and the schema and the objects differ. For plain row editing it only adds classes. It does not make the code faster, and the tool does not need to change its database.

quiz.question: A developer puts the rule that VIP customers get 10% off inside the CustomerMapper, because the mapper sees all the customer fields when it builds the object. Why is this a problem?
options: Mappers run too often, so the discount would be applied twice to every customer
The rule should have been put in the database, as a computed column of the table
Mappers are not allowed to change values, so the discount would not be saved to the row
The mapper's job is translation, and a rule in it is lost when a customer is built another way
quiz.explanation: A rule in the mapper only runs for objects that were loaded through it, and it ties business behaviour to storage. Rules belong in the domain object or a domain service. The other options describe problems that do not exist.
